title: THE BIBLE FORBIDS A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH A WOMAN AND HER GRANDDAUGHTER—WHY WOULD GOD GET THAT SPECIFIC?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE FORBIDS A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH A WOMAN AND HER GRANDDAUGHTER—WHY WOULD GOD GET THAT SPECIFIC?

Buried in Leviticus 18:17 is a disturbing command that reveals something much deeper about sexual sin, broken families, God's holiness, and the kind of grace that can rewrite even the most shameful human story.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are Bible verses that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper...
“Lord, why did You even have to say that?”
Leviticus 18:17 is one of them.
God specifically forbids a man from having sexual relations with a woman and her daughter or granddaughter.
Not merely a general warning against immorality.
Not simply a command to respect marriage.
God names the family relationships.
The daughter.
The son's daughter.
The daughter's daughter.
Three generations of women brought into one disturbing prohibition.
And suddenly, a question emerges that most people would rather avoid.
What was happening in the human heart that made such a command necessary?
But before you dismiss this as another strange Old Testament law, understand something.
This passage is not merely about ancient sexual behavior.
It is about what happens when desire stops recognizing boundaries, when people become objects of gratification, and when the very relationships meant to provide safety become places of betrayal.
And somewhere beneath this uncomfortable command is a truth that could expose something in our own generation.
Because the Bible does not always confront us where we expect.
Sometimes it confronts us where we have learned to make excuses.
And what begins as a disturbing verse in Leviticus eventually leads us to a Savior who refused to treat broken people as disposable.
Stay with this.
The uncomfortable part is not the end of the story.
Leviticus 18:17 says in the King James Version:

“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.”
Those words are unsettling.
But the Hebrew makes the meaning even more revealing.
The expression translated “uncover the nakedness” comes from the Hebrew phrase לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה — legalot ʿervah, meaning “to uncover nakedness.”
Within the sexual prohibitions of Leviticus 18, this is a conventional expression for prohibited sexual relations.
The language is not merely about accidentally seeing someone unclothed.
It addresses sexual boundaries.
And then comes another important Hebrew expression.
שַׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה — she'erah hennah.
In context, the words identify the women as closely related kin.
God is not treating these relationships as disconnected encounters between consenting strangers.
He is addressing the family bond itself.
Then the verse ends with a particularly forceful word:
זִמָּה — zimmah.
In this setting, it describes sexual wickedness or depravity.
The King James Version translates it as “wickedness.”
Other English translations use expressions such as “depravity.”
The Hebrew is morally weighty.
This is not simply an unusual arrangement that ancient Israel happened to dislike.
The law condemns it.
But here is where careful Bible reading matters.
The existence of a prohibition does not prove that every forbidden practice was widespread, nor does it tell us how often it occurred.
Scripture does not give us statistics about men taking sexual advantage of women and their granddaughters.
It does not tell us that every surrounding culture practiced this particular arrangement.
And we should never invent historical details just to make a sermon more dramatic.
What Scripture does tell us is that Israel was commanded not to imitate the practices of Egypt and Canaan (Leviticus 18:3), and that God established explicit boundaries around sexual relationships.
The specificity of the law serves a serious purpose.
It leaves less room for rationalization.
Because human beings can become remarkably creative when trying to justify what they already desire.
We rename things.
We minimize consequences.
We persuade ourselves that if something is possible, it must be permissible.
We tell ourselves nobody is being hurt.
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence a person can speak is...
“But the Bible never specifically said I couldn't.”
Leviticus 18:17 closes one such door.
It makes clear that a man cannot disregard the family relationships connecting these women and treat them as separate opportunities for sexual gratification.
The women are related.
That relationship matters.
And God's command recognizes it.
Now imagine the emotional damage that can occur when someone refuses to recognize such boundaries.
Imagine a family in which affection becomes tangled with rivalry.
Where trust is replaced by secrecy.
Where one generation fears what another generation knows.
Where the language of love becomes an excuse for exploitation.
Where someone who should have been protected is instead wounded.
These are possible consequences of boundary violations, not a claim that Leviticus describes one particular family tragedy.
But they help us recognize why sexual wrongdoing cannot always be reduced to a private decision between individuals.
Families are not collections of isolated bodies.
They are relationships of trust, responsibility, history, and belonging.
And when sexual desire disregards those realities, the consequences can reach far beyond the people immediately involved.
There is another important detail.
Leviticus 18:17 speaks of a woman, her daughter, and her granddaughter.
The passage is not exclusively a law about a man and his own biological granddaughter. It prohibits sexual relations with multiple generations within the same woman's family.
That distinction matters.
Because faithful interpretation does not exaggerate the text.
It listens to what God actually said.
The broader chapter also prohibits other close-kin sexual relationships, including relations involving a person's own descendants and relatives.
Together, these commands establish that sexual access is not unlimited simply because a person possesses desire, opportunity, or power.
And that brings us to a truth our generation desperately needs to recover.
A person can be desirable without being available.
A person can be vulnerable without becoming yours to exploit.
A person can trust you without giving you permission to cross a boundary.
And no amount of attraction transforms wrongdoing into righteousness.
But the deeper question is still waiting.
Why would a holy God concern Himself with something so intimate?
Why would the Creator of galaxies speak about sexual relationships inside a household?
Because the God of Scripture does not separate holiness from ordinary human life.
He cares about what happens in the bedroom.
He cares about what happens around the family table.
He cares about what happens when nobody else is watching.
He cares about the dignity of people whose pain might otherwise be hidden behind closed doors.
In Leviticus 18:2, God declares:
“I am the LORD your God.”
That statement establishes the authority behind the commands that follow.
Israel's sexual ethics were not meant to be governed merely by surrounding customs.
They were to reflect obedience to the God who had delivered them from Egypt.
Holiness was not simply about religious ceremonies.
It was about belonging to Him.
And belonging to God was meant to affect how people treated one another.
This does not mean every ancient Israelite perfectly obeyed.
The Old Testament repeatedly shows the opposite.
The Bible is painfully honest about human failure.
Consider the story of David.
A king with extraordinary privilege.
A man who knew God's law.
A man who had experienced God's mercy.
Yet when he saw Bathsheba, he chose to take what was not his.
Second Samuel 11 describes the devastating consequences of his actions, including his abuse of royal power and his arrangement of Uriah's death.
The prophet Nathan eventually confronted him.
And David's royal status could not make his sin righteous.
His spiritual history could not erase his accountability.
His power could not silence God's judgment.
David confessed in Psalm 51:4:
“Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight.”
David was not denying that he had sinned against other people.
He was acknowledging that his wrongdoing was ultimately an offense against God.
That is what makes biblical repentance so different from merely being embarrassed about getting caught.
Repentance does not ask only, “How do I repair my reputation?”
It asks, “What have I done before a holy God?”
And then it stops defending the indefensible.
Maybe that is where this passage becomes personal.
Not because you have committed the specific sin described in Leviticus 18:17.
Perhaps you never have.
Perhaps the very thought horrifies you.
But have you ever justified a boundary you knew you should not cross?
Have you ever hidden a relationship because you knew the truth would hurt someone?
Have you ever confused being wanted with being loved?
Have you ever told yourself that secrecy made something harmless?
Have you ever ignored a quiet conviction because obedience would cost you something?
The details may be different.
The underlying struggle with sin is painfully familiar.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That does not mean every sin is identical in severity or consequence.
It means no one can claim sinless righteousness before God.
The outwardly respectable person needs grace.
The person carrying a secret needs grace.
The person who has abused trust needs repentance and accountability.
And the person whose trust was violated needs to hear something just as clearly.
What someone did to you does not make you guilty of their sin.
If someone exploited you, manipulated you, coerced you, or violated your boundaries, their wrongdoing is not your shame to carry.
God's commands against sexual wrongdoing must never be turned into weapons against those who have been harmed.
The Bible's call to repentance addresses the wrongdoer.
It does not require victims to excuse abuse, remain in danger, or abandon justice.
And that distinction becomes especially important when we turn toward Jesus.
Because Jesus never treated sexual sin as insignificant.
But neither did He teach that a person's entire future must be permanently defined by the worst chapter of their past.
Consider John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
She has a complicated marital history.
Jesus tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
Notice what the passage does not tell us.
It does not explain why each marriage ended.
It does not authorize us to assume that she was responsible for every broken relationship.
And it does not invite us to invent a scandal greater than the one Scripture actually records.
What it does reveal is astonishing.
Jesus knows the truth about her life.
And He continues speaking with her.
He offers her living water.
He reveals Himself as the Messiah.
And the woman who came to draw water becomes someone who invites her community to encounter Christ.
John 4:29 records her invitation:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?”
Think about that.
Jesus knew her history.
Yet His knowledge did not prevent Him from offering her the truth about eternal life.
He did not need to pretend that her circumstances were simple.
He did not need to flatter her.
He did not need to hide who He was.
He met her in truth.
And He offered something greater than the water she had come to collect.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious slogan.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin is harmless. He saves sinners by dealing with sin through His own sacrifice.
The cross is not God's declaration that holiness no longer matters.
It is the place where God's justice and mercy meet.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired our lives.
Not after we had erased every consequence.
Not after we had made ourselves worthy of divine attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
New life is found in Him.
And those who belong to Him are called to turn from sin and walk in obedience.
Grace is not permission to keep destroying what God calls holy.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings us to Christ and begins transforming how we live.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
That means the Gospel does not merely change where we hope to spend eternity.
It changes how we are called to treat people today.
How we handle temptation.
How we respect boundaries.
How we honor marriage.
How we protect the vulnerable.
How we respond when confronted with our own wrongdoing.
And how we refuse to use spiritual language to excuse harm.
Perhaps someone reading this has spent years hiding behind a religious appearance.
You know the songs.
You know the verses.
You know how to lift your hands when the worship music begins.
But there is something in your private life you have refused to surrender.
Something you keep negotiating with God about.
Something you have renamed so many times that you almost believe the new name.
And perhaps this is the moment to stop negotiating.
Not because God is waiting eagerly to humiliate you.
But because hiding will never produce the freedom that truth and repentance can begin.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise is not an invitation to avoid accountability.
If your actions have harmed someone, repentance may require confession, ending harmful behavior, accepting appropriate consequences, and seeking help to ensure others are safe.
Forgiveness is not a substitute for justice.
And genuine transformation bears fruit.
But neither should you believe the lie that your past places you beyond the reach of Christ.
There is a difference between conviction and despair.
Conviction calls us toward the truth.
Despair tells us there is no point in returning.
The Gospel answers despair with the crucified and risen Jesus.
The One who said, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15) is also the One who gave His life to save sinners.
He does not offer cheap reassurance.
He offers redemption.
And if you have been wounded by another person's sin, hear this too.
Your healing does not have to follow someone else's preferred timeline.
You are not required to trust an unsafe person simply because they claim to have repented.
You are not less spiritual because you need support, distance, or protection.
Christ's compassion is not opposed to your safety.
And your story is not over simply because someone else damaged a chapter of it.
This is why we keep returning to the words:
Not because every consequence disappears.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because repentance magically restores every broken relationship.
But because the Gospel declares that sin, shame, and suffering do not possess ultimate authority over those who find their hope in Jesus Christ.
A person who has sinned can repent.
A person who has been wounded can seek healing.
A family that has experienced brokenness can pursue truth and restoration where it is safe and possible.
And a life that seemed hopeless can be transformed by the grace of God.
Leviticus 18:17 began with a boundary.
It confronted a form of sexual wrongdoing that violated family relationships.
But when we read it within the whole testimony of Scripture, it leads us toward a larger vision.
A holy God who cares about human dignity.
A righteous God who does not excuse evil.
A merciful God who calls sinners to repentance.
And a Savior who gave Himself so that forgiveness and new life could become possible.
The Bible is not embarrassed to speak about the darkness of human behavior.
Because God's answer to darkness is not to pretend it does not exist.
It is to bring truth into it.
And ultimately, to bring us to Jesus Christ.
Maybe this article did not expose the sin you expected.
Maybe it reminded you of something you have been avoiding.
Maybe it stirred memories of a wound you have never been able to explain.
Or maybe it simply helped you understand why a verse that seemed unnecessarily specific actually belongs to a much larger biblical concern for holiness, family boundaries, and human dignity.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave with curiosity alone.
Bring what you have discovered before the Lord.
Ask Him to search your heart.
Ask Him to reveal what needs repentance.
Ask Him to give you wisdom where relationships have become complicated.
And ask Him to teach you to love people in ways that honor their dignity rather than consume it.
You can simply write “Christ is still healing me” if you are holding on to His grace.
Or “No more hiding” if you are ready to walk honestly before God.
Or “Pray for me” if you are struggling and need encouragement.
You do not need to disclose private experiences, identify anyone who harmed you, or describe anything you are not ready to share. Even a quiet prayer matters.
And perhaps someone in your Facebook community needs to encounter this truth.
Not because they need to be publicly exposed.
But because they may be carrying a private battle that nobody sees.

Invite your family, your Christian friends, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for answers. There is room here for honest questions, biblical learning, repentance, encouragement, and growth.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing another inspirational message that disappears from your feed tomorrow.

Our desire is to continue creating Christ-centered articles, biblical studies, devotional materials, and discipleship resources that help people understand Scripture and grow in their walk with Jesus.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who may not have the means to purchase Christian learning materials.
People who are rebuilding their faith.
People who are hungry for the Word of God.
People who have questions they are afraid to ask.
People who need more than a passing motivational quote.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should be willing, not pressured.
And we want your decision to reflect that freedom.
You do not purchase God's favor.
You do not earn spiritual standing through a monthly payment.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith in everyday life.
It is helping the message continue.
It is supporting the creation of resources that can encourage believers, answer sincere questions, and point searching hearts toward Christ.
Following Gospel Warrior helps you stay connected with future teachings.
And inviting someone into the free library may give them access to resources they genuinely need.
Every faithful act of encouragement matters, even when no money changes hands.
Because ultimately, this is not about building an audience around a personality.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
The One who does not compromise holiness.
The One who does not abandon mercy.
The One who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And when you close this article, I hope you remember more than the strange specificity of an ancient command.
I hope you remember the God who gave it.
A God who takes human relationships seriously.
A God who sees what people try to hide.
A God who calls wrongdoing what it is.
And a God who sent His Son into a broken world so that sinners could be forgiven and transformed.
That is why the difficult passages matter.
They remind us that the Bible is not merely a collection of comforting statements.
It is God's Word, calling us to face the truth about ourselves and find our hope in Him.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth is this:
The same God who refuses to call your darkness holy is the God who sent His Son to lead you out of it.
